claims.text: Rapid cooling methods such as thermal quenching can control phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
Rapid cooling suppresses equilibrium phase transformations in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Rapid cooling stabilizes metastable microstructures in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
An as-cast or conventionally slowly cooled Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA exhibits equilibrium phase distributions.
High cooling rates affect nucleation rate, grain size, and phase-boundary mobility.
Rapid cooling limits atomic diffusion in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Limited atomic diffusion reduces the time available for equilibrium phase transformations.
Reduced time for equilibrium transformations promotes retention of metastable phases and alters the final microstructure.
Rapidly cooled samples will have a more refined microstructure than slowly cooled samples.
Rapidly cooled samples will contain less equilibrium-phase material than slowly cooled samples.
Rapidly cooled samples will contain more metastable-phase material than slowly cooled samples.
Conventional slow cooling permits full establishment of equilibrium phase distributions.
Rapid cooling may fail to prevent equilibrium phase formation when alloy composition strongly favors equilibrium phases.
Nonuniform cooling rates across a sample may reduce the effectiveness of rapid cooling for controlling phase evolution.
